These are my working notes on chip design, written the way I'd explain things to a friend. They're not polished, and they change as I learn. Notes link to each other, like Setup and hold time or Clock domain crossing. The graph shows how everything connects: click any dot to open that note. If something here looks wrong, I'd love to hear about it.

Every flip flop needs its input D to sit still for a short time around the clock edge. Setup time ( t {su} ): how long D must be stable before the edge. Hold time ( t h ): how long D must stay stable after the edge. Break either one and the flop can go metastable, which is also the core problem in Clock domain crossing. Setup check Data launched on one clock edge must arrive before the next edge, with setup time to spare: t {cq} + t {logic,max} + t {su} \le T {clk} + t {skew} If this fails, you can slow the clock, shorten the logic path, or split it with a pipeline stage. Hold check New data must not arrive too early and overwrite the value being captured on the same edge: t {cq} + t {logic,min} \ge t h + t {skew} Hold does not depend on the clock period, so slowing the clock never fixes a hold violation. The usual fix is adding delay (buffers) on the short path. Here t {skew} = capture clock arrival time minus launch clock arrival time.

A clock domain crossing (CDC) happens when a signal made on one clock is read by flops on a different, unrelated clock. The two clocks' edges have no fixed relationship, so sometimes the receiving flop samples the signal right while it changes. That breaks Setup and hold time and the flop goes metastable .

A systolic array is a grid of small, identical processing elements (PEs). Each PE does a multiply accumulate (MAC) and passes data to its neighbours every clock cycle, like a heartbeat pumping data through the grid. That's where the name comes from. The original roots stem from H T Kung's paper on Systolics, who is the same person who was involved in Brent Kung adders. I built a 4×4 one in Project Kalki.
